claims.text: The initial material system is an elemental Cr coating on a zirconium-alloy cladding substrate.
Al ion implantation at approximately 1×10^15–1×10^16 ions/cm² followed by annealing near 350°C will produce a graded Cr–Al layer.
Implanted Al will diffuse into the Cr coating during the 350°C anneal.
The graded Cr–Al layer will favor formation of Al2O3 under oxidizing conditions.
Oxidation of the modified layer will produce a dense, continuous oxide barrier.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be stable and passivating.
The surface Al2O3 barrier will increase the activation energy for Cr–Zr interdiffusion at the coating–substrate interface.
Increasing the activation energy for Cr–Zr interdiffusion will reduce atomic migration across the Cr/Zr interface.
Reduced Cr–Zr interdiffusion will preserve coating integrity and prevent premature failure.
Increasing Al content in an Al-containing coating on zirconium alloy can improve corrosion resistance and reduce oxygen penetration through formation of a denser oxide layer.
The Al-implanted Cr coating will exhibit less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than an unmodified elemental Cr coating.
The Al-implanted Cr coating will resist oxidation better than the unmodified Cr coating.
The Al-implanted Cr coating will resist cracking and maintain adhesion better than the unmodified Cr coating.
Unmodified elemental Cr coatings rapidly interdiffuse with Zr at elevated temperature, causing premature coating failure.
Approximately 320°C and 11.3 MPa water represent the proposed normal PWR exposure boundary.
Steam at approximately 1200°C for 1–2 hours represents the proposed accident-relevant exposure boundary.
The modified coating will remain protective during both prolonged PWR-water exposure and short-duration high-temperature steam exposure.
